CHAPTER 1.2 · LEARNING AREA 1

CHAPTER 1.2 · LEARNING AREA 1 · SEPTEMBER

Rates of change and the derivative

How fast is a stone falling at exactly this instant? How strongly is a bacterial culture growing right now? The answer is a local rate of change: the limit of the average rates of change. On the graph it is the gradient of the tangent, and the tangent is the best line that can hug the curve. In the advanced course you derive derivatives directly from the definition, including that of $a^x$, and in doing so you come across the number $e$.

WHAT YOU WILL LEARN IN THIS CHAPTER

  • understand the differential quotient as the gradient of the tangent and as the local rate of change
  • approximate a function near a point by its tangent: linear approximation
  • find derivatives from the definition, for $x^2$ and for $a^x$, sketch the derivative function and its graph and check differentiability

UNIT 15 LESSONS

1From the secant to the tangent

Between 1 and 2 seconds the stone falls $s(2) - s(1) = 15$ m, so 15 m/s on average. Between 2 and $2 + h$ it is $\tfrac{5(2 + h)^2 - 20}{h} = 20 + 5h$ metres per second. As the time interval gets shorter and shorter, this number approaches the instantaneous speed of 20 m/s.

KEY POINT · DIFFERENCE AND DIFFERENTIAL QUOTIENT

The difference quotient $\dfrac{f(x_0 + h) - f(x_0)}{h}$ is the gradient of the secant through $(x_0, f(x_0))$ and $(x_0 + h, f(x_0 + h))$, the average rate of change.

If its limit for $h \to 0$ exists, $f$ is called differentiable at the point $x_0$, and $$f'(x_0) = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{f(x_0 + h) - f(x_0)}{h}$$ is the differential quotient: the gradient of the tangent and the local rate of change.

The tangent $t(x) = f(x_0) + f'(x_0)(x - x_0)$ is the best linear approximation: $f(x_0 + h) \approx f(x_0) + f'(x_0) \cdot h$, and the error becomes small faster than $h$.

Notations: $f'(x_0)$ (Lagrange) and $\tfrac{\mathrm{d}f}{\mathrm{d}x}$ (Leibniz). For derivatives with respect to time, physicists write a dot: $\dot{s}$ (Newton).

Units: the rate of change has the unit “$y$-unit per $x$-unit”: metres per second, degrees per minute, euros per item.

INTERACTIVE · THE SECANT BECOMES THE TANGENT

Drag the second point towards the first. The difference quotient approaches the gradient of the tangent.

EXAMPLE 1 · INSTANTANEOUS SPEED

Find the speed of the stone with $s(t) = 5t^2$ after 2 seconds.

$\dfrac{s(2 + h) - s(2)}{h} = \dfrac{20 + 20h + 5h^2 - 20}{h} = 20 + 5h$.

Limit for $h \to 0$: $s'(2) = 20$ m/s, that is 72 km/h.

EXAMPLE 2 · LINEAR APPROXIMATION

Approximate $\sqrt{4.1}$ with the tangent to $f(x) = \sqrt{x}$ at $x_0 = 4$. We have $f'(4) = \tfrac14$.

$\sqrt{4 + h} \approx 2 + \tfrac14 h$, with $h = 0.1$: $\sqrt{4.1} \approx 2.025$.

Exact value $2.024\,846$: error only about $0.000\,15$.

INTERACTIVE · ZOOMED IN, EVERY CURVE IS STRAIGHT

Make the window smaller. Curve and tangent become indistinguishable, the error shrinks faster than $h$.

EXERCISES

Calculate the average rate of change of $f(x) = x^3$ on $[1, 3]$ and on $[1, 2]$.

$\tfrac{27 - 1}{2} = 13$ and $\tfrac{8 - 1}{1} = 7$

A tank is being filled: after 0, 2, 5 and 10 minutes it holds 0, 120, 270 and 420 litres. Calculate the average inflow rates in the three time intervals. What do you notice?

60 l/min, 50 l/min, 30 l/min. The inflow is getting weaker.

Find the local rate of change of $f(x) = \tfrac1x$ at the point $x_0 = 2$ with the limit of the difference quotient.

$\dfrac{\frac{1}{2 + h} - \frac12}{h} = \dfrac{2 - (2 + h)}{2(2 + h)h} = \dfrac{-1}{2(2 + h)} \to -\dfrac14$

Approximate linearly and compare with the calculator: a) $e^{0.1}$ with the tangent to $e^x$ at 0   b) $\sin 0.2$ with the tangent to $\sin x$ at 0. Give the relative errors.

a) 1.1 instead of $1.105\,17$, relative error about $0.47\,\%$   b) 0.2 instead of $0.198\,67$, relative error about $0.67\,\%$

Show for $f(x) = x^2$ and $x_0 = 1$: the error $f(1 + h) - t(1 + h)$ of the tangent is $h^2$. What does $\lim\limits_{h \to 0} \tfrac{h^2}{h} = 0$ mean for the quality of the approximation?

$t(x) = 1 + 2(x - 1)$, so $f(1 + h) - t(1 + h) = 1 + 2h + h^2 - 1 - 2h = h^2$. Relative to $h$ the error is arbitrarily small: no other line through $(1, 1)$ has this property, the tangent is the best linear approximation.

$20 + 5h \to 20$

UNIT 25 LESSONS

2The derivative from the definition

The quotients from the exploration tend to about 0.693 for the base 2 and to 1.099 for the base 3. In between there must be a base for which the limit is exactly 1: Euler’s number $e \approx 2.718$. The numbers 0.693 and 1.099 are $\ln 2$ and $\ln 3$.

KEY POINT · DERIVATIVE FUNCTION FROM THE DEFINITION

If you assign the number $f'(x)$ to every point $x$ at which $f$ is differentiable, you get the derivative function $f'$ with $$f'(x) = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{f(x + h) - f(x)}{h}$$

$f(x) = x^2$: $\dfrac{(x + h)^2 - x^2}{h} = 2x + h \to 2x$, so $f'(x) = 2x$.

$f(x) = a^x$: $\dfrac{a^{x + h} - a^x}{h} = a^x \cdot \dfrac{a^h - 1}{h} \to a^x \cdot \ln a$, so $\left(a^x\right)' = \ln a \cdot a^x$ and $\left(e^x\right)' = e^x$.

Differentiable ⇒ continuous, but not the other way round: $|x|$ is continuous at 0, but there the difference quotient is −1 on the left and 1 on the right.

Sketching the graph of $f'$: where $f$ increases, $f' > 0$; where $f$ decreases, $f' < 0$. Maxima and minima of $f$ become zeros of $f'$, the steepest points become extreme points of $f'$.

Why $e$? Only for the base $e$ is the exponential function its own derivative. That is why $e^x$ is the natural choice in science and engineering.

INTERACTIVE · THE DERIVATIVE OF aˣ

Change the base and make $h$ smaller. Green is the secant through $(0, 1)$, dashed is the tangent.

EXAMPLE 3 · FROM THE DEFINITION

Find the derivative function of $f(x) = \tfrac1x$ from the definition.

$\dfrac{\frac{1}{x + h} - \frac1x}{h} = \dfrac{x - (x + h)}{x(x + h)h} = \dfrac{-1}{x(x + h)}$

Limit for $h \to 0$: $f'(x) = -\dfrac{1}{x^2}$ for all $x \neq 0$.

EXAMPLE 4 · NOT DIFFERENTIABLE

Is $f(x) = |x|$ differentiable at the point 0?

Right: $\tfrac{|h|}{h} = 1$ for $h > 0$. Left: $\tfrac{|h|}{h} = -1$ for $h < 0$.

The one-sided limits are different: not differentiable. The graph has a kink at 0, but no jump.

INTERACTIVE · THE GRAPH OF THE DERIVATIVE APPEARS

Drag the point along the curve. The gradient of its tangent draws the graph of $f'$ point by point.

EXERCISES

Find the derivative function from the definition: a) $f(x) = 3x^2$   b) $f(x) = x^3$   c) $f(x) = 5x - 2$

a) $\tfrac{3(2xh + h^2)}{h} = 6x + 3h \to 6x$   b) $\tfrac{3x^2 h + 3xh^2 + h^3}{h} \to 3x^2$   c) $\tfrac{5h}{h} = 5$

Calculate $\tfrac{10^h - 1}{h}$ for $h = 0.001$ and compare with $\ln 10$. Give the derivative of $10^x$.

$\approx 2.3052$, $\ln 10 \approx 2.3026$. $\left(10^x\right)' = \ln 10 \cdot 10^x$.

Differentiate $f(x) = \sqrt{x}$ from the definition.

Multiply numerator and denominator by $\sqrt{x + h} + \sqrt{x}$ as in chapter 1.1.

$\dfrac{\sqrt{x + h} - \sqrt{x}}{h} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{x + h} + \sqrt{x}} \to \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{x}}$ for $x > 0$. At 0, $\sqrt{x}$ is not differentiable.

For $f(x) = x^3 - 3x$, sketch the graph of $f'$ without calculating $f'$. Then check with $f'(x) = 3x^2 - 3$.

$f$ has a maximum at $x = -1$ and a minimum at $x = 1$: $f'$ has zeros there, is positive outside and negative in between, with its minimum at 0. That is the parabola $3x^2 - 3$.

$f(x) = x^2$ for $x \leq 1$ and $g(x) = 3x - 2$ for $x > 1$ together form a function $F$. Is $F$ continuous at the point 1? Is it differentiable? What changes if you take $g(x) = 2x - 1$?

Continuous: both pieces give 1. On the left the gradient is $2 \cdot 1 = 2$, on the right 3: a kink, so not differentiable. With $2x - 1$ value and gradient match: continuous and differentiable, the line is the tangent to the parabola.

REVIEW · DEEPEN · CONNECT

Find the equation of the tangent to $f(x) = x^2$ at the point $(3, 9)$.

$f'(3) = 6$: $t(x) = 9 + 6(x - 3) = 6x - 9$

Connecting with chapter 1.1: explain why: if $f$ is differentiable at the point $x_0$, then $f$ is continuous there.

Write $f(x_0 + h) - f(x_0) = \dfrac{f(x_0 + h) - f(x_0)}{h} \cdot h$ and use the limit theorems.

For $h \to 0$ the first factor tends to $f'(x_0)$, the second to 0. By the product theorem, $f(x_0 + h) - f(x_0) \to f'(x_0) \cdot 0 = 0$, so $f(x_0 + h) \to f(x_0)$: continuous.

A bacterial culture grows according to $N(t) = 1000 \cdot 2^t$ ($t$ in hours). How fast is it growing after 3 hours? Give the result with $\ln 2$ and as a decimal.

$N'(t) = 1000 \cdot \ln 2 \cdot 2^t$, $N'(3) = 8000 \ln 2 \approx 5545$ bacteria per hour.

For which $a$ and $b$ is $F(x) = ax^2$ for $x \leq 1$ and $F(x) = 2x + b$ for $x > 1$ continuous and differentiable at the point 1?

Gradient: $2a = 2$, so $a = 1$. Value: $a = 2 + b$, so $b = -1$. Then $F(x) = x^2$ and $2x - 1$ respectively.

EXCURSIONHISTORY

Who invented differential calculus?

Isaac Newton developed his “method of fluxions” in the 1660s. His treatise “The Method of Fluxions” was finished in 1671, but he did not publish it. Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz found differential calculus independently and published it in 1684 in the Leipzig journal “Acta Eruditorum”, with the symbols $\mathrm{d}x$ and $\tfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}$ that we still use today.

This led to one of the most bitter priority disputes in science. In 1712 the Royal Society, whose president was Newton, investigated the question. Its report, the “Commercium epistolicum”, credited Newton with the invention and accused Leibniz of copying; Newton had helped to write it himself. Today the view is: Newton was earlier, Leibniz found it independently and published first. Newton’s fluxions only appeared in 1736, nine years after his death.

Sources: G. W. Leibniz: “Nova methodus pro maximis et minimis”, Acta Eruditorum, October 1684, pp. 467–473 · I. Newton: “The Method of Fluxions and Infinite Series”, London 1736 (written 1671) · Royal Society: “Commercium epistolicum D. Johannis Collins et aliorum de analysi promota”, London 1712.

LOOKING BACKTHE ESSENTIALS AT A GLANCE

DIFFERENCE QUOTIENT

$\tfrac{f(x_0 + h) - f(x_0)}{h}$: gradient of the secant, average rate of change.

$x^3$ on $[1, 3]$: 13

DIFFERENTIAL QUOTIENT

$f'(x_0) = \lim\limits_{h \to 0} \tfrac{f(x_0 + h) - f(x_0)}{h}$: gradient of the tangent, local rate of change.

$s(t) = 5t^2$: $s'(2) = 20$ m/s

LINEAR APPROXIMATION

$f(x_0 + h) \approx f(x_0) + f'(x_0) h$, the error becomes small faster than $h$.

$\sqrt{4.1} \approx 2.025$

FROM THE DEFINITION

$(x^2)' = 2x$, $\left(\tfrac1x\right)' = -\tfrac{1}{x^2}$, $(a^x)' = \ln a \cdot a^x$, $(e^x)' = e^x$

$\tfrac{2^h - 1}{h} \to \ln 2 \approx 0.693$

DIFFERENTIABILITY

One-sided limits of the difference quotient equal. Differentiable ⇒ continuous, not the other way round.

$|x|$ at 0: kink, not differentiable
